questions.prompt: When P-type and N-type silicon first touch, majority carriers diffuse across the junction. Why does that create net CHARGE near the junction?
options: The carriers that cross pile up as a charged layer exactly at the metallurgical junction
Electrons and holes are created at the junction by the contact
It doesn't; both sides stay neutral and only the potential changes
The carriers that leave uncover fixed dopant ions: negative acceptor ions on the P side and positive donor ions on the N side
questions.explanation:
Each region started neutral: every ion was matched by a free carrier. When holes leave the P side, the \(N_A^-\) ions they were neutralizing stay behind, uncovered and fixed. Likewise, electrons leaving the N side expose \(N_D^+\) ions (reader Sec. 5.4.1, 5.4.3).
The crossing carriers become minority carriers and quickly recombine; they don't build a layer. The resulting dipole (− on P, + on N) creates the junction's field and potential step.

questions.prompt: In equilibrium, which way does the built-in electric field point inside a PN junction (P side on the left, N side on the right)?
options: From the P side toward the N side (to the right)
There is no field in equilibrium, because no current flows
From the N side toward the P side (to the left, \(E < 0\))
It points up and down, perpendicular to the junction
questions.explanation:
Field lines start on positive charge and end on negative charge: from the \(+N_D\) ions on the N side to the \(-N_A\) ions on the P side, so to the left. Reader Fig. 5.4 plots it as negative, peaking at the junction.
It points from high potential (N) to low potential (P), and it pushes holes back toward P and electrons back toward N, opposing the diffusion.

questions.prompt: A PN junction has \(N_A = N_D = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Using the region potentials \(\varphi_n = \frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_D}{n_i}\) and \(\varphi_p = -\frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_A}{n_i}\), what is the built-in potential \(\varphi_{bi} = \varphi_n - \varphi_p\)? (\(kT/q = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\), \(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\))
questions.explanation:
\[\varphi_{bi} = \frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_AN_D}{n_i^2} = 0.026\ln\frac{10^{32}}{10^{20}} = 0.026\times27.63 \approx 0.718\ \mathrm{V}\]
Rule of thumb: 12 decades × 60 mV ≈ 0.72 V (reader Eq. 5.43–5.44).

questions.prompt: In thermal equilibrium, what is true of the four current components in a PN junction: electron drift, electron diffusion, hole drift and hole diffusion?
options: All four are zero, because nothing moves in equilibrium
Each is nonzero, but electron drift cancels electron diffusion, and hole drift cancels hole diffusion
Electron diffusion cancels HOLE diffusion, and the drifts cancel each other
Only the total is zero; electrons can carry net current one way and holes the other
questions.explanation:
Reader Eq. 5.14–5.17: \(J_n = qn\mu_nE + qD_n\frac{dn}{dx} = 0\) and \(J_p = 0\), each on its own. If, say, \(J_n = -J_p \neq 0\), electrons would continuously flow one way and holes the other. That would be a steady current loop with nothing driving it, which equilibrium forbids.
Carriers are constantly moving; the components only cancel on average.

questions.prompt: A junction has \(N_A = 10^{17}\) on the P side and \(N_D = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) on the N side. What is \(\varphi_{bi}\)? (\(kT/q = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\), \(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\))
questions.explanation:
\[\varphi_{bi} = 0.026\ln\frac{(10^{17})(10^{16})}{10^{20}} = 0.026\ln(10^{13}) \approx 0.778\ \mathrm{V}\]
Equivalently, it is \((kT/q)\ln(n_n/n_p)\): electrons drop from \(10^{16}\) on the N side to \(n_i^2/N_A = 10^{3}\) on the P side, which is 13 decades, or about 0.78 V.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives the charge density inside the junction's transition region, and what is its sign on each side?
options: \(\rho = q(p - n + N_D - N_A)\): negative on the P side (holes depleted below \(N_A\)), positive on the N side
\(\rho = q(p + n - N_D - N_A)\): negative on both sides
\(\rho = q(n - p + N_D - N_A)\): positive on the P side
\(\rho = 0\) everywhere, because the junction as a whole is neutral
questions.explanation:
Reader Eq. 5.18–5.24. On the P side \(n \approx 0\) and \(p < N_A\), so \(\rho \approx q(p - N_A) < 0\). On the N side \(p \approx 0\) and \(n < N_D\), so \(\rho \approx q(N_D - n) > 0\).
The junction as a WHOLE is neutral (the two charges are equal and opposite), but the local density isn't zero. That's exactly where the field comes from.

questions.prompt: Why don't majority carriers keep diffusing across the junction until the hole and electron concentrations are uniform everywhere?
options: Diffusion stops once the carriers reach the metal contacts
The carriers recombine as soon as they cross, so diffusion stops by itself
They do; in equilibrium the concentrations become uniform
The exposed ion charge builds a field whose drift current grows until it exactly cancels the diffusion; uniform carriers would leave the dopant ions hugely uncompensated
questions.explanation:
Diffusion builds the dipole, and the dipole's field drives drift the other way. Equilibrium is reached when the potential step is exactly \(\varphi_{bi} = \frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_AN_D}{n_i^2}\) (the Boltzmann relation from the carrier-potential skill).
Gotcha: recombination of the crossing carriers doesn't stop diffusion; it's what keeps the gradient there. Uniform carriers are impossible: the fixed dopants would then leave enormous net charge on each side.

questions.prompt: A junction has \(N_A = N_D = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). The P side's doping is raised 100 times, to \(10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). By how many mV does \(\varphi_{bi}\) increase? (\(kT/q = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\))
questions.explanation:
\[\Delta\varphi_{bi} = \frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_A'}{N_A} = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\times\ln(100) \approx 120\ \mathrm{mV}\]
Gotcha: 100 times more doping only adds about 0.12 V (two decades × 60 mV), because the dependence is logarithmic. Silicon junctions sit at roughly 0.6–1 V across a huge range of dopings.

questions.prompt: Inside the transition region, a few minority electrons from the P side (generated near the junction) wander into the field. Which way are they swept, and which way do holes drift?
options: Electrons are swept to the P side; holes drift toward the N side
Both drift toward the N side
Electrons are swept to the N side; holes drift toward the P side
Neither drifts; the field only affects majority carriers
questions.explanation:
The field points from N to P (\(E < 0\)). Electrons move against \(E\), toward N; holes move with \(E\), toward P.
So the junction field sweeps minority carriers ACROSS the junction (P-side electrons to N, N-side holes to P). That is the equilibrium drift current that balances diffusion. Under reverse bias it's what remains: the small saturation current.

questions.prompt: Preview of depletion widths: the uncovered charge on the two sides must be equal and opposite: \(qN_Ax_p = qN_Dx_n\). A junction with \(N_A = 10^{17}\) and \(N_D = 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) has a total depletion width \(x_p + x_n = 1.0\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). How wide is the N-side part, \(x_n\), in µm?
questions.explanation:
From charge balance, \(x_p/x_n = N_D/N_A = 10^{-2}\), so
\[x_n = W\frac{N_A}{N_A + N_D} = 1.0\times\frac{10^{17}}{1.01\times10^{17}} \approx 0.9901\ \mu\mathrm{m}\]
Almost the whole depletion region sits in the lightly doped side, because it needs more volume to uncover the same charge. The depletion-approximation skill turns this into a formula for the widths.

questions.prompt: Preview of contact potentials: a junction has \(\varphi_{bi} \approx 0.7\ \mathrm{V}\). You connect a wire from the P side to the N side. Does current flow?
options: Yes, about 0.7 V divided by the wire's resistance, until the junction runs down
No: the metal–semiconductor contacts develop their own contact potentials, which cancel φbi around the loop, so the junction is not a battery
Yes, but only while the junction is warm
Yes, a tiny current set by the diode's saturation current, forever
questions.explanation:
A steady current with no energy supply would be a perpetual-motion machine. The wire–silicon junctions are junctions between dissimilar materials too, and in equilibrium the potential steps around any closed loop sum to zero (reader Sec. 5.4.7).
The next skill works through this KVL. (Light, heat flow or an applied voltage are what break equilibrium and let a junction deliver or carry current.)

questions.prompt: Preview of diode behaviour: an external voltage makes the N side MORE positive than the P side (reverse bias), raising the barrier. What happens to the diffusion and drift currents?
options: Diffusion over the taller barrier drops exponentially, while the minority-carrier drift current stays about the same; a small net reverse current remains
Both grow in proportion to the voltage
Diffusion rises and drift falls
Both drop to exactly zero
questions.explanation:
Only carriers with enough energy can diffuse over the barrier. Their number goes as \(e^{-(\text{barrier})/V_{th}}\), so raising the barrier shuts diffusion off fast.
The drift current is set by how many minority carriers wander into the field, not by the barrier height, so it doesn't change. What's left is a tiny reverse current. Lower the barrier instead (forward bias) and diffusion grows exponentially: the diode turns on (reader Sec. 6.2).
